doc.title: Karl Berger interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, August 11, 2014

title: Music as architecture, audiences and Young Audiences
summary: Berger traces the shift from Wagner to music as sounding architecture, difficulty drawing audiences, and how sixth graders inspired Creative Music Studio.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: That’s terrific stuff. I really enjoyed that. You know the thing you said about the European free jazz became more about form —

Yeah. Well actually no, the new music. The whole music since Wagner. Wagner didn’t even call it music anymore. He called it tonkunst which means tonal art. So they were thinking more in terms of what an architect would think about. So music became like sounding architecture.
Does that alienate part of your audience? It’s like making it that much harder for the average listener?

No see like the problem that we have with the audiences is not so much — once there’s an audience there they are going to be very happy. Always. I have not seen an audience that walked away and didn’t like what we did. But to get them there, that’s our question. The problem is the industry has divided the music in such pieces that people don’t know anymore where the music really is. It’s not in a category anyway. Just because somebody played a certain category of music doesn’t mean it’s good or bad you know. And it’s very hard to get an audience to come and listen to you, just to actually come there.
You said something that I related to, when you did Young Audiences, back in the 70’s, that you felt the sixth graders at that point were ready to absorb anything.

Well it’s true. Like that sort of gave me one of the ideas to the Creative Music Studio because I realized that people are much more open to anything than you would ever imagine. Like we always have this idea everybody is sort of this personality and they are like set in their ways. But they’re set in their ways much later. But now it’s probably more like the fourth graders. You know when you go to a sixth grader now they are already inundated with all this iPhone stuff, and they probably think that music is what comes out of this little machine.
